paras: The whitecapping of Black log cutters at Thornton, Arkansas, was a warning delivered in the summer of 1895 by men described as 'whitecappers' to the Black employees of mill owner W. R. Pearson in Calhoun County, telling them they would no longer be allowed to cut logs. The notice halted Pearson's logging until he could find other labor, and Pearson attributed it to a determination to keep Black men from competing in mill work. The episode survives in a single Camden dispatch that ran in Arkansas state-news columns in early August.
Pearson, of Thornton, owned a large mill and 15 miles of railway and employed a large number of hands, among them Black men who cut logs for the mill.

According to a dispatch sent from Camden 'a few days' before August 2, Pearson reported that whitecappers in the county had notified his Black employees that they would not be allowed to cut logs any longer. As a result, work was suspended until he could procure other labor. Pearson gave his own view of the motive: he believed the parties involved were determined that 'the negroes shall not compete with them in mill work.' The dispatch does not name the whitecappers, say how many there were, or describe how the notice was given, and it reports no violence.
No report of arrests, an official response, or the workers' return was found in the coverage.

The Forrest City Times and the Monticellonian printed the item on August 2 under the headline 'Labor Troubles in Calhoun County', and the Osceola Times ran the same column the next day. In each paper it appeared as one short paragraph among routine state news, between a shooting near Pine Bluff and a railway incorporation, with Pearson's explanation repeated without comment.
The coverage found consists only of these white Arkansas weeklies; no Black-press account of the Thornton notice was found.

reader.title: Whitecapping of Black log cutters at Thornton, Arkansas
bases: Men described as 'whitecappers' notified the Black employees of a Thornton mill owner that they would not be allowed to cut logs, halting the work; no violence is reported (A1, A2).

The Thornton reports describe a warning that stopped Black men from working, with no killing or injury (A1, A2); the hanging of two Black men in Calhoun County noted by the Afro-American (A5) is not tied to Thornton, Pearson or the notice and is treated as a separate episode.
All three printings (A1, A2, A4) carry the same Camden dispatch word for word in a state-news column, so they are one report, not independent accounts; its source is the mill owner Pearson.

framing.detail: Treated as a labor item, 'Labor Troubles in Calhoun County', between local crime and business notes, with the employer's explanation given without comment.
No Black-press report of the Thornton notice was found; the Afro-American's 'The Curse of Lynching' condemned a separate Calhoun County hanging of two Black men.
